sentences.text: The single known species, Anthracosuchus balrogus, is known from four fossil specimens containing partial skulls.
Its armor consists of five osteoderms — bony plates embedded in the skin — that are thick and unpitted, unlike the flat, pitted plates of typical dyrosaurids.
Taxonomists classify this animal as one of the most basal dyrosaurids, placing it alongside Chenanisuchus and Cerrejonisuchus.
The species name 'balrogus' honors the Balrog from J. R. R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, a creature famous for dwelling in mines.
Robust, broad, and low-crowned teeth suggest a durophagous diet involving a crushing bite on hard-shelled prey.
Because its osteoderms do not overlap, the animal likely possessed greater flexibility than other dyrosaurs but suffered reduced stability.
The first fossil of Anthracosuchus was discovered in the Cerrejón mine in La Guajira, Colombia, in 2005.
Fossils of Anthracosuchus balrogus are found in the Cerrejón Formation within the Cerrejón mine.
The holotype specimen (UF/IGM 67) includes a nearly complete, dorsoventrally compressed skull, nine ribs, seven vertebrae, and unidentified bones.

The paratype (UF/IGM 68) contains a nearly complete uncompressed skull missing the premaxilla tip and right articular, three teeth, and postcranial elements including five osteoderms, five vertebrae, eight ribs, and parts of the pelvis.
Researchers suggest that Anthracosuchus may have practiced subsurface predation, differing from the feeding methods of other dyrosaurs.
The vertical muscle attachment on Anthracosuchus ribs suggests it swam with a more undulating motion than modern crocodylians.
Anthracosuchus lived during the Mid-Late Paleocene epoch.
The time range for Anthracosuchus is estimated from 61.66 to 56 million years ago.
